title: The Science of Context: How Do We Know
author: scienceofexplanation
summary: The Science of Explanation newsletter examines Bransford and Johnson's foundational 1972 cognitive science study on context and comprehension, which demonstrated that people cannot make sense of text -- even text composed of perfectly clear sentences -- without an organizing context provided before reading. The study showed participants meaningless-seeming paragraphs and found that when the context was provided before reading (not after), comprehension and recall were dramatically better. The piece extracts the educational implications: prior knowledge and advance organizers are not pedagogical niceties but cognitive prerequisites for learning. Without a schema to hang new information on, even well-written text produces minimal retention. The newsletter contextualizes Bransford and Johnson within the broader constructivist tradition (Ausubel, Piaget, Vygotsky) and argues that comprehension is not passive absorption but active construction -- a claim with direct consequences for instructional sequencing and background knowledge development.
points: * Bransford and Johnson (1972) demonstrated that context provided before reading dramatically improves comprehension and recall of otherwise meaningless text -- the same sentences are either opaque or transparent depending on whether a schema has been activated first. * Prior knowledge is a cognitive prerequisite for learning, not a pedagogical nicety: without a schema to organize new information, even clearly written text produces minimal encoding and near-zero retention. * The constructivist implication is that comprehension is not passive absorption but active construction -- the reader's existing knowledge structures determine what can be understood, and instruction that ignores those structures is inefficient. * Advance organizers (Ausubel) and activating prior knowledge are not warm-up activities but load-bearing elements of the lesson: they create the cognitive infrastructure that makes everything else possible. * The research has direct implications for background knowledge instruction: building the schema before teaching the text is not a luxury for enriched classrooms but a prerequisite for any instruction to work.
quotes: The Bransford and Johnson experiment is one of the most important things that has ever happened in cognitive science, and most teachers have never heard of it. They gave people a paragraph about doing the laundry without telling them it was about laundry. The paragraph was incomprehensible. Then they gave a different group the same paragraph with a picture of laundry or the word 'laundry' at the top. Same sentences. Completely different comprehension.

What the study showed, at the level of mechanism, is that comprehension is not something text produces in a reader. It is something a reader constructs from text plus what they already know. Take away the prior knowledge -- or fail to activate it -- and the construction cannot happen. The text just sits there.

Ausubel called the structure that makes new learning possible an 'advance organizer.' It is not an introduction. It is not background. It is a cognitive frame that tells the learner where the new information goes. Without the frame, new information has nowhere to go.

The implication for instructional sequencing is not subtle. You cannot teach a difficult text to students who lack the background knowledge to make sense of it. You cannot fix this with a better explanation or a clearer teacher. You cannot fix it by slowing down. You have to build the schema first, and that takes time, and that time is not wasted -- it is the work.

This is why background knowledge is not enrichment. It is the prerequisite. The students who arrive with more prior knowledge learn more from every lesson because every lesson builds on what they already know. The gap is not about vocabulary or decoding. It is about schema depth, and schema depth is built over years by being taught a lot about the world.
